summary: Paul Ekman studied at New York University (~1952–1954) and Adelphi University (~1954–1958). He held a post at the University of California, San Francisco from circa 1960 to 2004.

Active in religious and Buddhist studies, Paul F. Knitter studied at the Pontifical Gregorian University (~1958–1966) and the University of Marburg (~1969–1972). He held a post at Union Theological Seminary from circa 2007 to 2013.

A historian, Paul Fredericq studied at Ghent University and the University of Liège. He served as a professor at the University of Liège (1879–1883) and Ghent University, where he became rector in 1919.
Working in Buddhist studies, Paul Fuller completed his PhD at the University of Bristol under the supervision of Rupert Gethin, having also studied under Paul Dundas.

Specializing in Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and Indology, Paul G. Hackett studied at Columbia University. He held positions at the University of Virginia (attested 1994, 2003) and Columbia University (attested 2003, 2016).

Paul Groner, a scholar of Buddhist studies and Japanology, studied at the University of Tokyo and earned a PhD from Yale University. He served as a professor at the University of Virginia (attested 1982–1996, 2009–2010).

Indologist and philosopher Paul Hacker studied in Bonn, Heidelberg, Frankfurt, and Berlin. He held a professorship at Mithila Sanskrit Research Institute (1954) and chairs for Indology at the University of Bonn (1955–1963) and University of Münster (1963–1978).

Specializing in Buddhist and religious studies, Paul Harrison earned his MA at Auckland and PhD at Australian National University under Jan Willem de Jong and Tissa Rajapatirana. He later held posts at Auckland, Canterbury, and Stanford.
Historian Paul Hoswell Hardacre studied at Stanford University (~1933–1937) and UCLA (~1937–1947). He served as a historian of Stuart England at Vanderbilt University from circa 1947 to 1980.

Scholar of Buddhist studies, philosophy, and religion, Paul J. Griffiths studied at Oxford and Wisconsin-Madison under Minoru Kiyota. He held chairs at the University of Illinois Chicago (2000–2007) and Duke University (~2007–2017), among other appointments.
Paul Kingsbury, active in linguistics and Indology, completed his PhD at the University of Pennsylvania under the supervision of George Cardona (attested 2002).
A scholar in linguistics and Indology, Paul Kiparsky studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology under Morris Halle (~1962–1965). He held a post at Stanford University around 1984.

In Buddhist and religious studies, Paul Loren Swanson studied at Otani University and earned his PhD at Wisconsin-Madison under Minoru Kiyota. He served as a professor at Nanzan University from circa 1986 to 2021.

Specializing in religious studies, philosophy, and history, Paul Mendes-Flohr studied at Brooklyn College and Brandeis University. He held posts at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem (1999–2006) and the University of Chicago (~1999–2024).
A scholar of religion, Buddhism, and history, Paul Mus studied at Oxford, EPHE, INALCO, and the University of Paris. He held professorships at the Collège de France (1946) and Yale University (1951).
Active in Tibetology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies, Paul Nietupski earned his PhD from Columbia University and held an appointment at John Carroll University (attested 2008).
Linguist Paul Passy studied under Ferdinand de Saussure (~1885–1891) and held a post at the École Pratique des Hautes Études from circa 1894 to 1913.

A scholar of Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Tibetology, Paul Pelliot studied in Paris under Sylvain Lévi and Édouard Chavannes. He held posts at EFEO and the Collège de France (1911–1945).
Working in Indology and linguistics, Paul Regnaud was a student at the École Pratique des Hautes Études and later held a post at the University of Lyon from circa 1879 to 1908.
Philosopher and religious studies scholar Paul Ricœur studied at Rennes and Paris. He held academic posts at Strasbourg, Paris Nanterre, UCLouvain, and the University of Chicago (1970–1985).
